title: Persistent Prayer, Humility, and the Cost of Following

verses.text: Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart:
"In a certain town there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected men.
And there was a widow in that town who kept appealing to him, 'Give me justice against my adversary.'
For a while he refused, but later he said to himself, 'Though I neither fear God nor respect men,
yet because this widow keeps pestering me, I will give her justice. Otherwise, she will wear me out with her perpetual requests.'"
And the Lord said, "Listen to the words of the unjust judge.
Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night? Will He delay in helping them?
I tell you, He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?"
To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt, He also told this parable:
"Two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed, 'God, I thank You that I am not like other men— swindlers, evildoers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire.'
But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner!'
I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted."
Now people were even bringing their babies to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them. And when the disciples saw this, they rebuked those who brought them.
But Jesus called the children to Him and said, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.
Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it."
Then a certain ruler asked Him, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?"
"Why do you call Me good?" Jesus replied. "No one is good except God alone.
You know the commandments: 'Do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother.'"
"All these I have kept from my youth," he said.
On hearing this, Jesus told him, "You still lack one thing: Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me."
But when the ruler heard this, he became very sad, because he was extremely wealthy.
Seeing the man's sadness, Jesus said, "How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!
Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God."
Those who heard this asked, "Who then can be saved?"
But Jesus said, "What is impossible with man is possible with God."
"Look," said Peter, "we have left all we had to follow You."
"Truly I tell you," Jesus replied, "no one who has left home or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God
will fail to receive many times more in this age—and in the age to come, eternal life."
Then Jesus took the Twelve aside and said to them, "Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled.
He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon.
They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again."
But the disciples did not understand any of these things. The meaning was hidden from them, and they did not comprehend what He was saying.
As Jesus drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting beside the road, begging.
When he heard the crowd going by, he asked what was happening.
"Jesus of Nazareth is passing by," they told him.
So he called out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!"
Those who led the way admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, "Son of David, have mercy on me!"
Jesus stopped and directed that the man be brought to Him. When he had come near, Jesus asked him,
"What do you want Me to do for you?" "Lord," he said, "let me see again."
"Receive your sight!" Jesus replied. "Your faith has healed you."
Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Two prayer parables, teaching on the kingdom, a passion prediction, and a healing at the gates of Jericho
context.audience: The disciples (v.1), a group who trusted in their own righteousness and despised others (v.9), parents and children, a rich ruler, the Twelve, and a blind beggar with a crowd around him.
context.setting: Jesus is nearly at the end of the road to Jerusalem. The temple (v.10) is the setting of the Pharisee and tax collector parable, and the story ends at Jericho (v.35), about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem and the usual last stop for pilgrims coming up from the Jordan Valley.
context.custom: Pharisees fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays, and tithed carefully, so the Pharisee's claims in verse 12 are not exaggerations by the standards of his day. Beating the breast was a sign of deep grief and shame. Widows had little legal standing and relied on judges for justice, so a judge's indifference to one was a serious wrong. A rich man asking how to "inherit" life shows the common view that wealth was a sign of God's favor, which is why the disciples ask "Who then can be saved?" (v.26).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 17 ended with the days of the Son of Man. Chapter 18 opens with a parable about prayer in light of that waiting (v.8). It then moves through humility, children, the rich ruler, and a third prediction of the passion (v.31-33), before reaching Jericho. Luke 19 continues in Jericho with Zacchaeus.
context.timelineBible: The persistent widow echoes the biblical care for widows (Exodus 22:22-24, Isaiah 1:17). The prediction in verses 31-33 matches Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22, and it is the third time in Luke that Jesus tells the disciples about His suffering (9:22, 9:44). Bartimaeus's cry, "Son of David," is the first time in Luke that anyone gives Jesus this royal title in public.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus tells two parables on prayer: a widow who gets justice from an unjust judge by not giving up, and a Pharisee and a tax collector at the temple, of whom only the tax collector goes home justified. He welcomes children and says the kingdom must be received like a child. A wealthy ruler asks what to do to inherit eternal life and walks away sad when told to sell everything, leading to the camel and needle and the answer that what is impossible with man is possible with God. Jesus then tells the Twelve for the third time that He will be killed and rise, and they do not grasp it. Outside Jericho a blind beggar will not be silenced, calls Him Son of David, and receives his sight.

translation.meaning: To give up or grow weary in doing something good. Luke says the point of the widow parable is to keep praying and not quit.
Declared righteous before God. The word comes from the same family Paul uses for justification by faith. The tax collector, with nothing to offer but his plea, goes home in right standing.
Literally "be propitiated" or "be made favorable." The tax collector's prayer uses the language of atonement, as if he were standing under the sacrifices offered at the temple that day.
A title for the promised royal Messiah descended from David. A blind beggar names Jesus this while the crowd calls Him "Jesus of Nazareth," and he sees more clearly than they do.

otBackground.note: God hears the cry of the widow and the fatherless and promises to act.
David's cry, "Have mercy on me, O God," the pattern for the tax collector's prayer.
The commandments Jesus lists to the ruler, which he claims to have kept.
"Then the eyes of the blind will be opened." A mark of the Messiah's coming.
"Is anything too hard for the Lord?" The background to "What is impossible with man is possible with God."

commentary.note: Henry takes the key to the widow parable from its opening verse, that "men ought always to pray, and not to faint." If an unjust judge yields to persistence, the righteous Father will much more hear His elect who cry day and night. On the Pharisee and the publican, he says the one trusted in himself and despised others, and the other stood far off and pleaded for mercy, so that he "went down to his house justified rather than the other."

On the rich ruler, Henry says riches are a great hindrance: "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" He calls the camel and the needle a proverbial image of the extremely hard, and says salvation is impossible by human strength, but "the things which are impossible with men are possible with God." Of the blind man, he says: "Those who would speed in prayer must be importunate in prayer."

Gill says the widow parable is meant to encourage prayer so that believers do not faint under trials, and he argues from lesser to greater: if an unjust judge gives way, God will surely avenge His elect. Of the Pharisee he says he "prayed only with respect to himself." On the rich ruler, he notes that riches are "often a bar unto a profession of Christ." He sees the blind man's persistence as an example for all who seek Christ, and notes that after his healing he followed Jesus, "since none but God could do this."

overview.summary: Jesus teaches persistent prayer through a widow and a judge, and humility through a Pharisee and a tax collector. He welcomes children, and a rich ruler walks away sad. Near Jericho, He predicts His death and heals a blind beggar.
overview.settingLine: The road to Jerusalem, ending near Jericho.

history.t: Tax collectors worked for Rome and were hated, as the one in the temple shows.
It lay about 15 miles from Jerusalem, the last stop before the long climb.

customs.t: Widows had few legal protections, so a widow pleading with a judge was truly powerless.
Pharisees fasted Mondays and Thursdays and tithed carefully, so his claims were real.

archaeology.t: Ancient Jericho's mound is among the oldest cities known, but Jesus' Jericho lay nearby.
Herod's winter palaces near Jericho have been excavated, with pools and gardens.

overview.discussion: The Pharisee thanked God he wasn't like others. How do we avoid his trap without a new kind of pride?
